title: tai simpson:
title_q: “I’m Telling a Good Story With My Life”
title_short: tai simpson · A Good Story With My Life
headline: The board president is her tribe’s storyteller. Supporting NIWRC, she says, is how she tells a good story with her life: not only the loss, but the culture, the language and the laughter.
story: tai simpson (she writes her name in lowercase; her language has no capital letters) is NIWRC’s board president and a citizen of the Nimiipuu, the Nez Perce. She runs the Idaho Coalition Against Sexual and Domestic Violence. Near the end of the interview she asked to add one thing, and it is the whole cut: in her tribe she is known as the storyteller, and her job is to live a good story and pass it on.

The cut opens on that line, names the stakes in her own family, and lands on what she wants the world to see: aunties and grandmas laughing together is healing too. Do not use her “life-givers” passage (04:59 to 05:37). That idea is Lucy Simpson’s cut (NIWRCOKCLucySafetyIsNotAbsence001).

Loops: L1 “What does a storyteller have to do with this?” opens at 0:00 and closes at 0:13 (“stories that I share to the next generation”). L2 “What is the good story?” opens at 0:00 and closes in the BUTTON (“our art and our laughter”). Stakes: she is a descendant of women who experienced violence in her community.
do: Open on her mid-sentence with the hook text on frame 1.
Let her finish her sentences. She speaks in full thoughts.
Use C1 as the main picture and C2 for one cutaway. Sound from C1 only.
Caption the Nez Perce words as (speaks in her language). Do not try to spell them.
Write her name in lowercase on the super: tai simpson.
Use only the files named here.
dont: No logo, name or fade at 0:00.
No stock footage, no regalia montage, no historical images. Stay on her and the room.
Do not use the life-givers passage (04:59 to 05:37). It belongs to Lucy’s cut.
Do not use Event 17 (Are You Happy block). It belongs to the AYH series.
No Tribal affiliation on the super. Name and title only.
No number or statistic on screen.

--- 26-10-09 C1 Happy - NIWRC Event 13.MP4 ---
[00:12] Ty Simpson: My name is Ty Simpson and I am the board president of the National Indigenous Women's Resource
[00:21] Ty Simpson: Center.
[00:22] Ty Simpson: I'm a citizen of the Ninipu tribe, commonly called the Nez Perce tribe.
[00:26] Ty Simpson: I'm from northern Idaho, by way of Atlanta now.
[00:34] Ty Simpson: Ty is T-A-I.
[00:36] Ty Simpson: Simpson is S-I-M-P-S-O-N, like the TV show.
[00:40] Ty Simpson: Come through, they'll edit.
[00:51] Ty Simpson: Good to see you all.
[00:55] Ty Simpson: Thank you.
[00:56] Ty Simpson: Yes, I stylize my name in lowercase.
[00:58] Ty Simpson: Thank you.
[00:58] Ty Simpson: Because there's no capitalization in my language.
[01:06] Ty Simpson: That's why he's here.
[01:10] Ty Simpson: Alright, so when I ask you a question, you repeat it a little bit to me.
[01:13] Ty Simpson: Okay.
[01:14] Interviewer: Like I said, what did you have for dinner?
[01:15] Interviewer: You said, what was the dinner I had?
[01:17] Interviewer: Whatever.
[01:18] Ty Simpson: Thank you.
[01:19] Interviewer: Alright, what called you to serve on this board and what made you take on the chair?
[01:25] Ty Simpson: I was called to serve on the NIWRC board by some of the aunties that have been in the organization
[01:31] Ty Simpson: for anywhere between 10 to 12 years.
[01:33] Ty Simpson: I have been running the Idaho Coalition Against Sexual and Domestic Violence since 2019,
[01:40] Ty Simpson: so it was an opportunity to step into leadership that was specifically engaging native women and girls,
[01:46] Ty Simpson: and that was appealing to me because I am a native woman and was once a native girl.
[01:50] Ty Simpson: I'm also a descendant of women who've experienced violence in my community,
[01:55] Ty Simpson: and when I showed up to my first meeting, we were in Arizona,
[01:58] Ty Simpson: and I wasn't expecting to take on a leadership role, but was asked to take on leadership
[02:04] Ty Simpson: because of how politically and policy driven that I've been in state coalition spaces,
[02:10] Ty Simpson: and I think that translates well to an organization like NIWRC.
[02:15] Ty Simpson: I'm bridging some gaps, making sure that communities who are not historically involved in policy work
[02:23] Ty Simpson: and in anti-violence work have the biggest, loudest mic at the table.
[02:29] Ty Simpson: So that's my job, and that's why I was called to serve.
[02:31] Ty Simpson: This is one earring.
[02:36] Ty Simpson: They'll move around a lot.
[02:37] Ty Simpson: No, you're good. I didn't know if they're bad or not.
[02:39] Ty Simpson: Like you were showing, like, all pink.
[02:42] Ty Simpson: Thank you.
[02:43] Ty Simpson: You're welcome.
[02:44] Interviewer: You want to answer that again?
[02:45] Ty Simpson: No, no. We can move on. Thank you.
[02:48] Ty Simpson: Thank you.
[02:56] Interviewer: What do you want the next generation to inherit from this movement?
[03:01] Ty Simpson: I think in our communities, we really try to work in such a way where the future generations
[03:07] Interviewer: have something really strong to inherit and to work from.
[03:10] Ty Simpson: This movement has been taking place since colonization, since first contact.
[03:15] Ty Simpson: We really sought to start to rally in the mid-1900s, and then as we saw legislation like VAWA and VOCA
[03:22] Ty Simpson: being passed in the 70s and 80s, it rallied Native women, mothers, grandmothers, aunties, and sisters
[03:28] Ty Simpson: to drive policy that positively impacted wellness and safety for Native women.
[03:34] Ty Simpson: And so I hope the work that we're doing at NIWRC and this generation is more around making our voices louder
[03:41] Ty Simpson: in policy places and spaces, making sure that our communities are well-resourced with the right finances
[03:48] Ty Simpson: and tools to be safe, and really starting to engage the broader community in understanding that
[03:54] Ty Simpson: protecting Native women and girls, in fact, creates safety for our communities everywhere.
[04:02] Interviewer: What have you seen change in tribal communities because of this movement?
[04:07] Ty Simpson: Oh my goodness, there's so many changes that we can celebrate across the country from the work of NIWRC.
[04:14] Ty Simpson: I'm thinking about policy changes that we've made, how much the shift that the Office of Violence Against Women
[04:22] Ty Simpson: has made in supporting Native communities in the way that we do this work.
[04:25] Ty Simpson: The expansion into Alaska and Hawaii are big changes as well.
[04:30] Ty Simpson: And I also think that the very intentional inclusion of Native women in Congress, both federally and at the state level,
[04:38] Ty Simpson: our voices as Native women in national initiatives around safety and wellness is also indicative of the fact that
[04:45] Ty Simpson: we've made some sweeping revolutionary changes in just our generation.
[04:51] Interviewer: Why does it matter that this organization is Native women-led?
[05:00] Ty Simpson: NIWRC is Native women-led for a number of reasons, and I think that our deep cultural alignment to nature and to land
[05:09] Ty Simpson: is a good reason why we energize that sort of leadership.
[05:13] Ty Simpson: A lot of our nations, we believe that water is life-giving as women are life-giving, that Earth and nature is life-giving as women are
[05:20] Ty Simpson: life-giving.
[05:21] Ty Simpson: So when we talk about the safety of Native women and girls, it is life-givers who can speak to those challenges,
[05:27] Ty Simpson: to those obstacles, to our needs, and to our futures.
[05:31] Ty Simpson: And so to ensure that NIWRC stays Native women-led is really going to be kind of this powerful mechanism
[05:37] Ty Simpson: for changing safety and wellness for all of our communities.
[05:45] Interviewer: Can you tell I was a beauty queen?
[05:47] Interviewer: Were you?
[05:48] Ty Simpson: I was, like way back.
[05:50] Interviewer: What did NIWRC make possible that would not happen with others?
[05:57] Ty Simpson: Oh man, Tilly Blackbear got us to a place that would have been impossible in the 70s and 80s.
[06:04] Ty Simpson: Her intentional energy behind grassroots organizing to interrupt violence against Native women and girls was life-changing,
[06:11] Ty Simpson: not only for her tribe, but for all of our tribes across the country.
[06:15] Ty Simpson: She ensured that our voices were heard at tables and rooms that we were never invited to,
[06:19] Ty Simpson: that our names and our tribes and our issues were spoken to at all legislative levels.
[06:25] Ty Simpson: She made sure that our communities were funded and funded well and funded sustainably.
[06:30] Ty Simpson: We are standing on the shoulders of giants when it comes to the aunties who energized this work early on.
[06:36] Ty Simpson: And in this generation, we're grateful for the way that they informed this work and for their input and for their wisdom.
[06:44] Ty Simpson: And I think that, you know, I think that for the future, and I think that for our communities in general,
[06:55] Ty Simpson: we've really got to remember that we have been organizers in our communities just culturally and spiritually
[07:02] Ty Simpson: without any external guidance, without any external pressure, and that's worth celebrating
[07:07] Ty Simpson: because it wouldn't be that way in a system that's not designed to involve us.
[07:15] Interviewer: The last question, is there anything that you want to add?
[07:20] Ty Simpson: Yes, yes.
[07:21] Interviewer: Okay, what do you want to add?
[07:22] Interviewer: I'm going to add, do you want me to contextualize it first?
[07:25] Ty Simpson: Oh, yeah, give it to me.
[07:26] Ty Simpson: Okay, no.
[07:27] Interviewer: Do you want me to ask you a question to start it?
[07:28] Ty Simpson: Oh, no, I got it, I got it.
[07:30] Ty Simpson: In my culture, in my tribe, I'm known as the storyteller.
[07:32] Ty Simpson: Inamunikwa sakti kwatit.
[07:35] Ty Simpson: And so my responsibility as a cultural storyteller and a culture keeper is to make sure that the stories that have been passed to
[07:41] Ty Simpson: me over generations
[07:43] Ty Simpson: are stories that I share to the next generation.
[07:45] Ty Simpson: And it's not just telling the story, but living my life in such a way where I'm telling a good story with my life.
[07:51] Ty Simpson: And so I think that participating and supporting what NIWRC does is telling a good story for the future,
[07:57] Ty Simpson: that it's not just about all of our loss and the violence and the land theft and the sordid history that we have with
[08:06] Ty Simpson: the United States,
[08:07] Ty Simpson: but it's also about celebrating our culture and our language and our music and our dance and our art and our laughter.
[08:12] Ty Simpson: If you're ever in a room with native aunties and grandmas and the way that we all laugh together is also incredibly healing
[08:19] Ty Simpson: and also worth celebrating in the work that we're doing.
[08:22] Ty Simpson: Good job.
[08:24] Ty Simpson: I got to tell you, that was the end of that segment, so I have one question for one of you.
[08:29] Ty Simpson: This one's going to be directly answered.
